title: Publishing glass: distinct material publication forms for microscope slides
research_problem: The Cole case shows that a slide can be part of a serial publication. The wider source base shows several other ways in which prepared microscopic objects were issued, replicated, numbered, catalogued and made retrievable. These forms should be compared without calling every distributed slide a 'publication'.
definition_guard: Use 'material publication' only when distribution is structured by an explicit repeatable issue/series/set system, public catalogue, or replicated numbering scheme. A unique slide sent in correspondence, a private cabinet, a teaching collection, and a museum accession are circulation forms but are not automatically publications.

forms.case: Arthur C. Cole, Studies in Microscopical Science
forms.unit: one issue combining preparation + letterpress + image
forms.replication: subscribers receive materially similar but explicitly non-identical biological preparations
forms.time_structure: weekly full stream made from two interleaved fortnightly tracks; later monthly sections
forms.relation_to_print: simultaneous and directive: prose tells the subscriber what to inspect in the accompanying preparation
forms.distinctive_problem: glass copies cannot be identical in the way printed copies can, so plate/text calibrate material variability

forms.case: Farlow Herbarium published diatom collections, including nineteenth-century slide series
forms.unit: numbered specimen/slide within a named published collection
forms.replication: the same set-specific serial number is distributed in replicate collections to different institutions or users
forms.time_structure: set/edition distribution rather than recurring periodical cadence
forms.relation_to_print: catalogue/list/card or accompanying documentation can identify each number; print need not be issued weekly with the object
forms.distinctive_problem: replicate sets make the number portable across geographically separate collections; later institutional catalogues may preserve or replace it

forms.case: Norman 1872, Bourgogne 1862, Möller and other preparation catalogues
forms.replication: maker may produce multiple examples of the advertised object, but catalogue row does not guarantee a fixed edition identity
forms.address: catalogue title/number or subject description; maker/retailer label
forms.relation_to_print: catalogue describes what can be purchased; the purchased slide may later retain only fragments of catalogue wording
forms.distinctive_problem: catalogue identity, commodity identity and physical object identity must be distinguished
forms.evidence_strength: S for catalogue systems; object matching varies

forms.unit: ordered histological sections from one embryo or specimen
forms.replication: sections are sequential parts of one anatomical series rather than copies distributed to subscribers
forms.address: series/card number + slide/part sequence; later HEC and MCZ identifiers
forms.relation_to_print: specific series can be cited/figured in publications, but the collection is primarily a research archive
forms.distinctive_problem: seriality alone does not make a publication; this is a useful control against overextending the Cole thesis

forms.replication: expected distributed set logic; exact edition/replicate architecture to verify from series documentation and surviving La Plata set
forms.relation_to_print: catalogues/provenance tables potentially map numbers to slides
forms.distinctive_problem: needs object-level and documentary verification before being described with the same precision as Farlow's explicitly documented published collections

forms.case: Haeckel correspondence, society donations, private exchanges
forms.unit: one or several physical preparations sent between named people/institutions
forms.address: letter date/sender/recipient + object description; later label or accession
forms.relation_to_print: may later support research/publication but is not issued as a repeatable public series
forms.distinctive_problem: circulation should not be redescribed as publication merely because the object moves

diagnostic_questions: Was there an explicitly named series, set, issue or catalogue?
Could more than one recipient obtain an object under the same public address?
Was the address stable across distributed copies/replicates?
Did text/image/documentation accompany the object synchronously, or only describe it in a separate catalogue?
Was the material object meant to be read/observed in a prescribed sequence?
Does the surviving museum number preserve the original distribution address or replace it?
Are two slides with the same number intended as replicas, serial sections, catalogue variants, or entirely different address namespaces?

comparative_payoff.cole_article: Cole remains distinctive because print, image and preparation are synchronized at issue level, and subscriber preparations are allowed to vary materially while remaining publication equivalents.
comparative_payoff.farlow_comparator: Farlow's published/unique collection distinction supplies an explicit historical-collection ontology: replicated numbered sets versus unique collections acquired by gift, exchange or purchase. This is an unusually strong external control for defining material publication.
comparative_payoff.tempere_next_step: Use La Plata to establish whether Tempère & Peragallo's surviving numbers behave like replicated published-set addresses, catalogue numbers, or a different hybrid.
comparative_payoff.book_history_implication: Bibliographic description of material publications needs fields for physical component, replicated-set identity, serial number, accompanying print, distribution form and surviving crosswalk; title/author/date alone are insufficient.
